title: Ang 857–858: Namdev, Ravidas, Sadhna
tomorrow: what's smaller than a sesame seed, and never wasted?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's joy: mad with praise, and glad of it. Today three more Bhagats close Bilaval, and one of them talks back.

Some people pray like writing a thank-you card. Some pray like a text sent at one in the morning: are you even there? On ang 858, Sadhna does the second. In paraphrase: if my karma isn't wiped away, Guru of the world, then what is your greatness? Why seek a lion's shelter, if a jackal eats me anyway?
screen: `A THANK-YOU CARD.` → `A TEXT AT ONE A.M.` → `WHAT IS YOUR GREATNESS?`

segments.voice: Bilaval closes with three Bhagats. Namdev first, in paraphrase: the Guru made my life fruitful. Then Ravidas: people saw my poverty and laughed; now powers rest in my palm, all by your grace. And his second hymn: whatever family a true devotee is born into, high or low, rich or poor, their fragrance spreads through the world. Then Sadhna, blunt. Beyond the lion and the jackal, in paraphrase: the rainbird suffers for one drop of water; once life is gone, an ocean is no use to it. Sikhs read this two ways. The first view: this is love talking. The Bhagats speak to God the way you speak to someone close, frankly, even demanding, because they trust the relationship can hold it. The Granth kept these words, after all. The second view: the Gurus keep teaching hukam, living inside God's will, and a demand like "what's your greatness?" is the cry of someone in pain, honored for its honesty and answered by surrender. Look how Sadhna ends, in paraphrase: I am nothing, I have nothing; protect my honor now, I'm your servant. The first view hears a friend's bold words. The second hears a cry that turns into trust. Both agree on one thing: the Granth gave it a place.
screen: `NAMDEV: A FRUITFUL LIFE.` · `RAVIDAS: THEY LAUGHED; NOW GRACE.` · `SADHNA: WHAT IS YOUR GREATNESS?` · `TWO READINGS, ONE PLACE IN THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `THREE CLOSE IT.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one honest question you'd put to God or to life right now, as plainly as Sadhna did. Fold it once and hold it for the sit, not answering it, just letting it be said. If you'd like, read his hymn on ang 858 first.
Ang 857. Where Namdev, Ravidas and Sadhna close raga Bilaval, with one blunt question at the very end.
Three close it: a fruitful life, a fragrance from any family, and a question asked straight out. Bilaval, done.
